title: Answering a Visitor's Questions on the Conditions for Rebirth
author: Zhanran
excerpt: Q: Why is it that one can be reborn only with right mindfulness at the end of life (ten successive recollections at the end of life)? Amitābha Buddha's five kalpas of reflection and measureless kalpas of practice, and his entire great vow, are all for the deliverance of every living being. With such great compassion, would he not, at the moment of our death, exercise his majestic vow-power to come and receive us?

inline.s: Ten Recollections at the End of Life — Continuous Recollection Brings Rebirth

Q: Why is it that one can be reborn only with right mindfulness at the end of life (ten successive recollections at the end of life)? Amitābha Buddha's five kalpas of reflection and measureless kalpas of practice, and his entire great vow, are all for the deliverance of every living being. With such great compassion, would he not, at the moment of our death, exercise his majestic vow-power to come and receive us?
A:

At the moment of every living being's death, Amitābha Buddha is there to receive them; it is only that those without right mindfulness at the end of life cannot see him, and so they follow their own deluded thoughts and are reborn according to their karma.
Therefore, one must have right mindfulness at the end of life in order to see Amitābha Buddha come to receive one, and then follow the Buddha to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
On this principle, Master Zhongfeng, honored as the Ancient Buddha of Jiangnan, teaches in the *Three-Period Liturgy of Tying the Mind*:
“Although it is said that Amitābha gathers in living beings for rebirth, you must believe
that it is only a manifestation from your own mind
a sympathetic resonance
, ultimately
(in the final analysis)
not something obtained from outside

[Only a manifestation from your own mind] Amitābha Buddha's coming to receive (gather in) living beings is only a manifestation from your own mind; this is due to sympathetic resonance, and is not something obtained from outside. Therefore only those with right mindfulness at the end of life can see the Buddha coming, while the other people around them cannot see him. For those beings who are inverted at the end of life, because their own minds are turbid and disordered, they lack the feeling of right mindfulness (ten successive recollections); naturally Amitābha's reception will not appear in response within their minds, and so they cannot see the Buddha come,
and it is not that Amitābha Buddha has not come to receive them
The *Buddha Speaks of the Sūtra of Immeasurable Life* says:
“Its land
does not turn against or reject
(the Land of Ultimate Bliss does not refuse any living being rebirth there)
, drawn along by what is natural
(those living beings who are not reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss naturally follow their own deluded thoughts at the end of life and are reborn in the six paths)
Therefore, whether one is reborn or not depends entirely on whether one has right mindfulness at the end of life
(ten successive recollections at the end of life)
This is why
both Master Shandao, who was Amitābha Buddha come again, and Master Yongming, who was Amitābha Buddha come again, earnestly teach:
you must accomplish ten successive recollections at the end of life
(see
The Eighteenth Vow
for details)
. This is, after all, Amitābha Buddha's own teaching!
[Sympathetic resonance] The feeling of living beings and the response of Amitābha Buddha interpenetrate one another.

[(On) those living beings who are not reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss naturally following their own deluded thoughts at the end of life and being reborn in the six paths] On this, Master Lianchi teaches:
Those who are inverted at the end of life,
because in their daily lives they follow along with deluded thoughts and do not cultivate right mindfulness, have minds that are much scattered. At the time of relinquishing the sensation of warmth
(at the time of the dissolution of the four great elements)

, everything they have done in their whole life appears before them; their minds are terrified and their movements are thrown into disorder. Those who should enter the hells see the mountains of knives and trees of swords as beautiful gardens. Those who should fall into the animal realm take the bellies of horses and wombs of donkeys for splendid halls. Even those who have done good and should be born among humans or gods cannot avoid loving or hating their parents. Even the lesser sages at the initial stage of the first fruit cannot rightly know their entering and exiting. All of these are what is called inversion. Riding on this inversion, in the three realms and the seven destinies they are reborn according to their karma. ...... Just as the Buddha said: ‘When the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure.’ And again: ‘All lands are upheld only by thought.’ When pure thoughts are accomplished, one will surely attain rebirth, without any doubt.”

(from the *Commentary and Subcommentary on the Amitābha Sūtra*) Translation: Those who are inverted at the end of life are all those who, in their daily lives, follow along with deluded thoughts and do not cultivate right mindfulness, their minds much scattered. At the time of the dissolution of the four great elements, everything they have done in their whole life appears before them, and their minds are terrified, their conduct thrown into disorder. Those who should enter the hells see the mountains of knives and trees of swords as beautiful gardens. Those who should fall into the animal realm take the bellies of horses and wombs of donkeys for splendid halls. Even those who have done good and should be born in the human or heavenly realm cannot help but love the mother and hate the father when born male, or love the father and hate the mother when born female. Even those at the initial fruit of the Lesser Vehicle and bodhisattvas at the initial resolve still have the delusion of the intervening existence and cannot rightly know their entering and exiting the womb. All of these are inversion. Because of this inversion at the end of life, one is reborn in the seven destinies of the three realms according to one's karma. ...... Just as the Buddha said: ‘When the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure.’ (When the mind is pure, the Buddha-land in which one is born is also pure.) The Buddha also said: ‘All lands are upheld only by thought.’ (All lands are upheld entirely by the mind's thoughts.) Therefore, when a Buddha-reciter's pure thoughts are accomplished, he will surely be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. On this, of course, there is not the slightest doubt. [Seven destinies] Hell, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, immortals, gods, and asuras. “Destiny” (qù) means the direction toward which one tends. [Buddha-land] The territory taught and transformed by a single Buddha, divided into the pure land, the defiled land, the reward land, and the land of Dharma-nature.
On the principle of sympathetic resonance at the end of life, Master Yinguang, who was Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva come again, teaches in the *Preface to a Beginner's Guide to Pure Karma*:

“The minds of living beings are like water, and Amitābha Buddha is like the moon. When living beings are complete in faith and vows and move the Buddha with utmost sincerity, the Buddha responds, just as the moon appears when the water is clear. If the mind is impure and insincere, in accord with greed, anger, and delusion and turned away from the Buddha, then, like water that is turbid and stirred, although the moon does not fail to shine upon it, it cannot clearly reflect the moon's image.”

Translation: The minds of living beings are like water, and Amitābha Buddha is like the moon. When living beings are complete in faith and vows and move the Buddha with utmost sincerity, the Buddha responds — just as the moon appears when the water is clear and still (a metaphor for the pure mind of right mindfulness evoking the appearance of Amitābha's reception). If the mind is impure and insincere, in accord with greed, anger, and delusion and turned away from the Buddha, then, like water that is turbid and stirred, although the Buddha-moon shines upon it without omission (a metaphor for Amitābha always receiving every living being at the end of life), it cannot clearly reflect the image (a metaphor for the stirred and turbid mind being unable to evoke the appearance of Amitābha's reception,
but instead following its own deluded thoughts and being reborn according to its karma

“Only when the water is clear and still does the moon appear; when the water is turbid and stirred, it is hidden. The moon, of course, has no picking or choosing; the reason it does not appear is that the water is turbid and rushing, and so cannot receive its reflected image.”

Translation: Only when the water is clear and still does the moon's reflection appear; when the water is turbid and stirred, the moon's reflection does not appear. The moon, of course, shines without any picking or choosing; the reason it does not appear is that the water is turbid and rushing, unable to present the moon's reflection. (Metaphor: Only those living beings who have right mindfulness at the end of life can see Amitābha's reception, while those without right mindfulness at the end of life cannot see Amitābha's reception. Amitābha Buddha, of course, receives every living being at the end of life without picking or choosing; the reason those without right mindfulness at the end of life cannot see Amitābha's reception is that
their own minds are turbid
and scattered,
and so
they follow their own deluded thoughts and are reborn according to their karma

Therefore, for the Buddha-reciter, right mindfulness with a single mind at the end of life is of the utmost importance. Reciting a thousand times, ten thousand times, even reciting all day and all year long, is nothing other than to make this one thought of Buddha-recitation mature,
so as to ensure that at the end of life this thought continues without break and evokes the appearance of Amitābha's reception
. Therefore, both Master Shandao, who was Amitābha Buddha come again, and Master Yongming, who was Amitābha Buddha come again, earnestly teach:
you must accomplish ten successive recollections at the end of life
(see
The Conditions for Rebirth
This is the measure of the sages' words! If one does not listen to Amitābha Buddha's own words, whose words is one to listen to?

[Continuous] The thought of Buddha-recitation succeeds one another without mixing in deluded thoughts. [Measure of the sages' words] This is spoken by the sages, correct and without error, and can certainly be believed and accepted.
Q: There is a saying: “Even if one recites the Buddha's name with a scattered mind, as long as faith and vows are complete, one will surely be reborn.” Is this saying correct?
A: Both the Buddha and the patriarchs have repeatedly taught us to recite the Buddha's name with a single mind, and have repeatedly urged us to practice as taught (see
A Commentary on the Sūtra in Praise of the Pure Land
). Therefore, those complete in faith and vows certainly practice as taught and recite the Buddha's name with a single mind (see
Single-Minded Buddha-Recitation, Not Scattered-Minded Recitation
). The scattered-minded reciter is one who, precisely because he dreads difficulty and hardship, practices contrary to the Buddha's and the patriarchs' teaching;
this is precisely the concrete manifestation of faith that is not true and vows that are not earnest
(see the teaching of Master Yongming, who was Amitābha Buddha come again, below). Therefore,
the scattered-minded reciter,
as Master Yongming said, is one of
“weak and slight faith.”
Hence, the scattered-minded reciter's faith and vows are certainly not true and earnest
. The situation of “scattered-minded recitation together with true faith and earnest vows” simply does not exist;
it is a false proposition,
just as there is no such thing as a brave warrior who cowers before battle.

Since such a situation does not even exist, how can there be any talk of rebirth or not? Therefore, “even with scattered-minded recitation, as long as faith and vows are complete, one will surely be reborn” is simply an absurd fallacy.
[False proposition] A proposition that is not true. [Proposition] A declarative sentence that expresses a judgment.
Master Yongming
in
the *Collection of the Ten Thousand Good Deeds Returning to the One*
teaches:
“If one's words and deeds do not match,
the power of faith is weak and slight,
with no mind of thought after thought in continuity, but a mind of repeated interruptions
(that is, scattered-minded recitation)
Relying on such laxness,
at the end of life one hopes for rebirth, but is obscured by karmic obstructions, and will likely fail to meet good spiritual friends; pressed by wind and fire,
right mindfulness will not be accomplished
In this teaching, Master Yongming clearly points out: why does one recite with a scattered mind (
“with no mind of thought after thought in continuity, but a mind of repeated interruptions”
)? It is because of
“words and deeds not matching, the power of faith weak and slight.”
Therefore, one whose words and deeds match and whose faith and vows are true and earnest will certainly recite the Buddha's name with a single mind.
And scattered-minded recitation precisely shows that this person is one of
“words and deeds not matching, weak and slight faith.”
Moreover, Master Yongming particularly points out that scattered-minded recitation is a lax practice; going on in this lax way (
“relying on such laxness”
), at the end of life,
“pressed by wind and fire, right mindfulness will not be accomplished”
and therefore one will not be reborn
[Words and deeds not matching] Words and deeds do not match: verbally one claims to have true faith and earnest vows, but one's actual conduct is lax (neither true nor earnest):
“no mind of thought after thought in continuity, but a mind of repeated interruptions.”
